name: 6-OXO (4-androstene-3,6,17-trione)

lead: 6-OXO is an oral supplement ingredient described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor. Steroid and prohormone users have taken it to limit estrogen and gynecomastia.
The main human study was small, uncontrolled and partly industry-funded; it found hormone changes but no change in body composition.

paras: Reported to permanently inactivate aromatase, lowering estradiol and raising LH and testosterone.
The FDA stated products containing it are adulterated, and Health Canada warned in 2008 of a blood-clotting risk. Acne is a listed possible effect. It is banned by WADA.

lead: 6-OXO (4-androstene-3,6,17-trione, also 4-AT) is an oral supplement ingredient described as a potent, irreversible aromatase inhibitor that may raise the testosterone-to-estrogen ratio [1]. It has been used mainly by people using steroids or prohormones, who say it limits estrogen rise and gynecomastia risk, and after cycles to shorten recovery of testicular function [1].

The main human study is a 2007 eight-week trial in resistance-trained men that reported large rises in free testosterone and DHT but no change in body composition; it had no control group and was partly funded by commercial producers [1]. The FDA and Health Canada have issued warnings about products containing it [1].
infobox: FDA warning letter 2006; Health Canada warning 2008; banned by WADA [1]

paras: 6-OXO is described as permanently inactivating aromatase in fat and peripheral tissue. Lower estradiol is reported to raise luteinizing hormone and, in turn, testosterone [1]. Wikipedia notes that testosterone is myotropic while estradiol is not, but that no human or animal studies have tested whether 4-AT has an anabolic effect [1].

Users, often of steroids or prohormones, report taking it to offset estrogen increases during a cycle, which they say reduces gynecomastia risk, and afterwards to shorten recovery from testicular suppression [1].

Analytical papers in 2005 described detection of 4-AT and its metabolites in urine, and the World Anti-Doping Agency bans it [1]. A 2006 FDA warning letter argued that marketing it violated federal law, and the FDA stated that products containing it are adulterated under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act [1]. In 2008 Health Canada warned of a blood-clotting risk and told users to stop; acne is listed as a possible side effect [1].

A 2007 Baylor University study gave 300 mg or 600 mg per day to resistance-trained men for eight weeks and reported large rises in free testosterone and DHT and a higher testosterone-to-estradiol ratio, with no effect on body composition or safety markers. It had no control group and was partly funded by commercial 4-AT producers [1].
